teaser.text: Phillips 66 is an energy company that buys raw materials, turns them into fuels and industrial ingredients, and moves them to customers. To understand its business, follow what it sells, how it earns a margin or a fee, and who pays along the chain.

blocks.heading: What has to go right or wrong for Phillips 66?

paragraphs.text: Phillips 66’s price path is modestly positive by October 2027 but negative by October 2029; it hinges on normalized refining earnings, execution, and cash available for debt reduction and buybacks. Management targets adjusted controllable refining costs of $5.50 per barrel by 2027 and at least $1,000 million of additional mid-cycle adjusted EBITDA from Midstream and Chemicals. It promises to return at least 50% of net operating cash flow to shareholders during 2026–2027 and targets total debt of $17,000 million by 2027.

The bear case reflects realized refining margins falling from $17.26 per barrel in 2023 to $8.84 in 2024. The bull case assumes tighter supply, better market capture and partial delivery of the $5.50-per-barrel cost target and $1,000 million Midstream and Chemicals EBITDA target.

blocks.heading: How much cash does Phillips 66 really make?

paragraphs.text: Subtracting $220 million of stock compensation produces “real free cash flow.” That is an analytical measure: issuing shares does not consume cash immediately, but it still transfers value from existing owners to employees.

blocks.heading: What does an investor pay for Phillips 66 today?

paragraphs.text: Revenue has fallen from its 2022 peak while operating margin and the company’s own free-cash-flow margin move with the cycle. In 2025, reported earnings improved, but adjusted net income was $2,632 million and asset-sale gains lifted the reported result. Shareholders received $1.38 per share more than free cash flow after dividends and buybacks. At $297.29, Phillips 66 has a 16.9x trailing P/E and a 9.7x forward P/E, against a 2.3% free-cash-flow yield and 1.7% dividend yield. Market value is $118,625 million; enterprise value is $135,091 million. Free cash flow is the company’s own figure: cash from operations minus capital spending.

blocks.heading: How much does Phillips 66 pay in dividends?

paragraphs.text: In 2022, free cash flow was $8,925 million. Shareholder payments were $3,306 million. The balance looked very different in 2024: free cash flow was $2,332 million, while shareholders received $5,333 million. Buybacks, which are purchases of the company’s own shares, fell from $3,451 million in 2024 to $1,207 million in 2025. Dividends were steadier.

The dividend starts at $5.08 per share, matching the current $1.27 quarterly rate. The base case raises it to $5.28 and $5.48; the bear case freezes it; the bull case reaches $5.36 and $5.64. The base path follows the record of annual increases while recognizing that the 50% cash-return target does not specify dividend growth.

blocks.heading: Does Phillips 66's cash cover its dividend?

paragraphs.text: The company also recycled assets. In 2025, businesses and assets sold brought in $3,520 million. Acquisitions cost $3,498 million. That looks broadly self-funding, but shareholders still received $3,129 million against free cash flow of $2,729 million. Asset sales can finance purchases, but they do not prove that the remaining businesses generated enough spare cash.

Phillips 66 generated substantial cash in 2025, but investment and timing reduced what owners could freely claim. Operating cash flow was $4,962 million in 2025. Capital spending was $2,233 million, leaving free cash flow of $2,729 million.

earnings.title: Phillips 66 earnings: October 28, 2026
earnings.meta_description: Phillips 66’s October 28, 2026 results: guidance, recent revenue and profit, and the operating and cash details to watch.
earnings.opening: Phillips 66’s next results are expected on October 28, 2026. For Phillips 66, the key thing to watch is whether turnaround expense, Corporate & Other costs and cash reconciliation match guidance.
earnings.closing: The full memo also answers questions about Phillips 66’s business, rivals, management and risks.

paragraphs.text: The immediate commitment is $2,370 million of capital expenditures and investments for 2026. Capital spending buys assets that last for years; sustaining capital keeps the current system working, while growth capital expands it. Midstream receives $1,100 million and Refining receives $1,080 million. Chevron Phillips Chemical Company, or CPChem, the chemicals joint venture, has a separate $680 million allocation that it is expected to fund itself.

Finally, management promises to return at least 50.0% of net operating cash flow to shareholders during 2026–2027. It also aims for total debt of $17,000 million and net debt below 30.0% of capital by 2027. Because working-capital movements are excluded from the return calculation, the targets must be met through repeatable operations. That makes analysts’ earnings expectations the next part of the story.

blocks.heading: Has Phillips 66 kept its past promises?

paragraphs.text: Phillips 66 returned $13.6 billion against a stated distribution commitment of $13 billion–$15 billion through year-end 2024. It also reported $1.5 billion in annualized cost and capital reductions, while acknowledging that its net-debt-to-capital ratio exceeded its target. Annualized savings describe the yearly benefit at the achieved pace, not cash already saved for a full year.

blocks.heading: What are Phillips 66’s last eight quarters of revenue and profit?

paragraphs.text: The second quarter of 2026 showed a genuine operating recovery, amplified by hedges and working-capital timing. Revenue rose from $33,323 million to $51,004 million against the prior-year quarter.

blocks.heading: What should I watch in Phillips 66’s next results?

paragraphs.text: The next checkpoint is the October 28, 2026 results call. Investors should compare Q3 turnaround expense of $100–120 million and Corporate & Other costs of $325–350 million with actual results, then follow the cash reconciliation.
